slides.title: The loop: how a model writes an answer
slides.summary: The model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and runs again on the longer text. It stops when its best guess is the end token.
body: Give the model “The pizza is ready” and ask what comes next. Each run of the model does the same job: turn the text into vectors, pass them through the transformer's layers, and score every possible next token. The second figure below shows one run in full.

ul: Run 1 reads “The pizza is ready” and picks “ for”.
Append it. The input is now “The pizza is ready for”, one token longer.
Run 2 reads all of that, including the word it just wrote, and picks “ you”. Then “!”, one token per run.

body: <mark>The model never writes a whole answer at once. Every token comes from a full run over everything so far, including the tokens it has already written.</mark>

body.h: How does it know it's finished?

body: It doesn't decide in any deep sense. Every answer in its training data ended with a special end token, so once a reply looks complete, that token becomes the most likely prediction. When it wins, the loop stops.

ul: The end token wins: the usual way a reply ends.
A length limit: the app caps the number of tokens, which can cut a reply off mid-sentence.
A stop sequence: the app can also stop when a chosen piece of text appears.

body.note: Each run uses attention to let the newest token look back at everything before it. That's what the rest of this chapter explains.

body.more: Isn't re-reading the whole text every run slow?
body.text: It would be. Models keep the work already done for earlier tokens in a KV cache, so each run only has to compute the newest token.
body.link: The KV cache in Output & inference

body.more: What does the end token look like?
body.text: It's one of the tokenizer's special tokens, such as <|endoftext|> in GPT-2. Chat models use an end-of-turn token from their chat template.

steps.caption: The model gets the token IDs of the text so far.

item.label: The pizza is ready for
item.sub: run 1 read 4 tokens and picked “ for” (42%)

steps.caption: The winner is appended. The input is now one token longer.

item.label: The pizza is ready for you
item.sub: run 2 read 5 tokens and picked “ you” (58%)

steps.caption: The model runs again on everything, including its own last word.

item.label: The pizza is ready for you!

item.label: end token
item.sub: run 4: the reply looks complete, so the end token wins (81%)

figure.alt: The generation loop for "The pizza is ready". Run 1 reads The, pizza, is, ready and predicts " for" at 42%; it is appended. Run 2 reads the five tokens and predicts " you" at 58%; appended. Run 3 reads six tokens and predicts "!" at 47%; appended. Run 4 reads "The pizza is ready for you!" and predicts the special end token at 81%, so the loop stops and the reply is finished. Finishing is just one more prediction: answers in training ended with an end token, so the model learns to predict it once a reply is complete. Apps also stop at a length limit. Probabilities are illustrative.
figure.caption: Each run's winner joins the input for the next run. The reply ends when the end token wins.

figure.alt: How an LLM predicts the next token for "The pizza is ready". 1: split into tokens The, space pizza, space is, space ready. 2: look up token IDs, 791, 23317, 374 and 5644 in GPT-4. 3: turn IDs into vectors of numbers, plus position. 4: run the transformer: N identical layers, each with layer norm, self-attention, where ready looks back at every earlier token, layer norm and a feed-forward network; then layer norm and linear plus softmax, giving one score per vocabulary token. Self-attention is this chapter. 5: score every possible token, for 42%, to 31%, at 12%, now 6%, and pick one, giving The pizza is ready for. 6: add it to the text and run again, one token at a time. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: One run in full, from text to the next token. Attention, the highlighted box, is what the rest of this chapter explains.

slides.title: The big idea: tokens read each other
slides.summary: Attention lets each token pick up information from the other tokens it needs, so words get their meaning from the words around them.
body: After the lookup step, each token's vector knows nothing about its neighbours. "Bank" has the same vector in "river bank" and "bank account". To understand text, a token has to look at the words around it.
Attention is how it does that. Each token builds a new vector that takes its context into account, by pulling in information from the other tokens that matter to it.
Every token plays three roles at once:

ul: Query: what this token is looking for. Something like "I'm an adjective; which noun do I describe?"
Key: what this token offers, used for matching. "I'm a noun."
Value: the information this token hands over if it's chosen.

body: Each query is compared with every key. <mark>Good matches get big weights, and the token's new vector is a mix of the matching values.</mark>

body.note: A database lookup returns the one row whose key equals your query. Attention returns a mix of every row, weighted by how well each key matches. Because nothing is all-or-nothing, the model can learn it by making small adjustments.

body: The next four slides work through this step by step on "I am learning artificial", with real numbers.

figure.alt: Each token vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to make queries, keys and values. Every query is compared with every key to give a grid of scores. Scores for future tokens are masked out. Softmax turns each row into weights that add up to 1, for example "artificial" puts 36 percent of its weight on "learning". Each token's output is the weighted mix of the value vectors.
figure.caption: The map for this chapter. The next four slides compute each step with real numbers.

slides.title: Step 1: make Q, K and V
slides.summary: Three learned matrices turn each token's vector into a query, a key and a value.
body: Each token's vector x is multiplied by three different learned matrices, giving three new vectors for each token:

ul: Q = x·Wq: the query. What am I looking for?
K = x·Wk: the key. What do I contain?
V = x·Wv: the value. What will I hand over if picked?

body: These are ordinary matrix multiplications, the "many dot products at once" from The big picture. Nobody designs Wq, Wk and Wv by hand. Training adjusts them until queries and keys find useful connections.
To keep the numbers readable, each token here has 4 numbers (d_model = 4) and each Q, K or V vector has 3 (d_head = 3). Real models use thousands, and 64–128.

body.note: Each row of the Q table is one token's query. Green cells are positive, red cells are negative, and stronger colour means a bigger number.

code: q, k, v = Wq(x), Wk(x), Wv(x)    # each [B, n, d_head]

slides.title: Step 2: score every pair
slides.summary: Every query is compared with every key using a dot product. This gives a grid of scores showing how relevant each token is to each other token.
body: Now compare every query with every key using a dot product. For 4 tokens, that gives a 4 × 4 grid of scores, written S = Q·Kᵀ. (Kᵀ means K transposed: flipped on its side so the multiplication lines up.)
Read the grid one row at a time. Row i shows how relevant each token is to token i. A high score means token i's query matches that token's key well.

Dot products of long vectors give big numbers. Big scores make the next step (softmax) put almost all the weight on one token, and then the model barely learns. Dividing by the square root of the vector length (here √3) keeps the scores in a sensible range.

body.note: The grid has one entry for every pair of tokens, so n tokens give n² entries. Double the length of the text and you get four times the work. That's where attention's famous O(n²) cost comes from.

slides.title: Step 3: no peeking ahead
slides.summary: A mask stops each token from looking at later tokens. That's what makes next-token training work.
body: GPT, Claude, Llama and other chat models are decoder-only models, trained to predict the next token. If a token could see the one after it, predicting it would be too easy: the model would just copy the answer.

So every score above the diagonal, where a token would look at a later token, is set to −∞ (minus infinity). In the next step those become exactly 0: no attention to the future. This is called the causal mask.

There's a big bonus. Since no token can see ahead, one pass over a training sentence trains every position at once: position 1 predicts token 2, position 2 predicts token 3, and so on, all at the same time.

Encoder models like BERT, used for sorting text into categories and for search, skip the mask and look both ways. That's great for understanding a finished sentence, but they can't write text one token at a time. Switch the mask on and off to compare.

slides.title: Step 4: softmax, then mix the values
slides.summary: Softmax turns each row of scores into weights that add up to 1. The output is a mix of the values, using those weights.
body: Each row of scores becomes attention weights using softmax: raise e (≈ 2.718) to the power of each score, then divide each result by their total. The weights are all positive and add up to 1, like percentages.

body.note: Scores [2, 1, 0] become e² ≈ 7.39, e¹ ≈ 2.72 and e⁰ = 1, which add up to 11.11. So the weights are 0.67, 0.24 and 0.09. The biggest score gets the most weight, but the others still get some. A masked score of −∞ becomes e<sup>−∞</sup> = 0.

body: Each token's output is then a weighted sum of all the value vectors: out = softmax(S)·V. If "artificial" puts 36% of its weight on "learning", then 36% of its new vector comes from the value of "learning".
Pick a query row on the right to see where that token looks and what it gets back.

body.note: That's all attention is: compare (Q·K), turn into weights (softmax), mix (·V). The rest of this chapter is about doing it many times side by side, and doing it fast.

slides.title: Multi-head attention
slides.summary: Models run many small attention steps side by side, so each one can track a different kind of connection.
body: A single attention pattern has to choose where to look. <mark>But a token often needs several kinds of information at once: the previous word, the subject of the sentence, a matching bracket far back in some code.</mark>

So models run h attention heads side by side, each with its own Wq, Wk and Wv. To keep the cost the same, each head uses smaller vectors: d_head = d_model / h. A model with d_model = 4,096 and 32 heads gives each head 128 numbers.
Each head gives its own output. These are joined end to end and mixed by one more learned matrix, Wo.

body.note: Picture a team reading the same document, each person looking for something different, who then share their notes.

body: Researchers who study what happens inside models (interpretability) find heads that specialise. The four patterns on the right are simplified versions of common ones. The first-token pattern is real and has a name, an attention sink: a place where heads put their weight when nothing else is relevant.
code: q = q.view(B, n, h, d_head).transpose(1, 2)  # [B, h, n, d_head]
out = attention(q, k, v)                     # per head

slides.title: Why attention is expensive, and the fixes
slides.summary: Attention's work grows with the square of the text length. A few clever tricks keep it under control.
body: The score grid has n² entries for every head in every layer. At 1,000 tokens that's a million scores per head. At a million tokens, it's a trillion. Drag the slider to watch it explode.
Three common fixes:

ul: FlashAttention gets exactly the same result, but works in small chunks that fit in the GPU's fast built-in memory, so the full grid is never stored. Same maths, much less slow memory access. It's now the default in major frameworks.
Grouped-query attention (GQA): several query heads share one set of key and value heads. Quality stays nearly the same, and the KV cache (see Output & inference) gets several times smaller.
Sliding-window and sparse attention: some layers only look back a fixed distance, or at chosen positions, instead of at everything.

body.note: <mark>This is why long prompts are expensive.</mark> Even with these tricks, a 200,000-token prompt needs far more computing and memory than a 2,000-token one.

code: # PyTorch picks a fused kernel (e.g. FlashAttention) when it can

slides.title: Position in depth: the wave pattern
slides.summary: Attention on its own ignores word order. The original Transformer fixed that with position vectors built from waves at different speeds.
body: Now you can see why attention needs position. Each token scores every other token with a dot product of a query and a key, and nothing in that calculation depends on where the tokens sit. Leave out the mask and shuffle the input, and every token gets the same scores, just in a different order.
Embeddings showed the fix: add a position vector to each token's vector. Here is how the original Transformer (2017) built those vectors.

ul: Each pair of numbers in the position vector follows a wave (a sine and a cosine) at its own speed, from very fast to very slow.
To get position 5's vector, read every wave at position 5. That is the stamp added to the token there.
Fast waves tell neighbours apart; slow waves tell near from far.

body: <mark>Every position gets a unique vector, nearby positions get similar ones, and every value stays between −1 and +1, so the position never drowns out the word.</mark>

body.note: Think of a clock with many hands. The second hand alone can't tell you the time. But seconds, minutes, hours and days together mark every moment uniquely, and moments close together look alike.

body.more: Why not just add the number 5?
body.text: Token vectors hold small numbers, roughly between −1 and +1. Adding 5,000 for a late position would swamp the word's meaning. Dividing by the text length instead would make position 5 mean different things in short and long texts. Waves avoid both, and need no training.

body: In the heatmap, each row is a position and each column one number: fast-changing columns on the left, slow ones on the right.

figure.alt: Why models need position, and how the original Transformer added it. First, without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" contain the same three tokens, so attention alone gives the same result for both. Second, with position, every token is stamped with its place in the sentence, 0, 1 or 2, so "dog at position 0" and "dog at position 2" become different inputs: the input is the token vector plus a position vector. Third, the position vector comes from waves at different speeds. Four waves are drawn across positions 0 to 16, from the fastest to the slowest. Reading all four waves at position 5 gives that position its own stamp: about −0.96, +0.60, +0.89 and +0.43. Nearby positions get similar stamps.
figure.caption: Without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same to attention. A position vector, read off waves at different speeds, stamps each token with where it sits.

slides.title: RoPE: what modern models use
slides.summary: Modern models mark position by rotating vectors, so attention can directly see how far apart two tokens are.
body: Most current open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen and others) use rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead. Nothing is added to the token's vector. Instead, inside attention, each token's query and key are rotated by an angle that grows with the token's position.

Why rotate? Attention scores two tokens with a dot product, and the dot product depends on the angle between the two vectors. Rotate one by position m and the other by position n, and the angle between them only depends on m − n: how far apart they are.
Try it: move both sliders by the same amount. Both arrows turn, but the angle between them, and so the score, doesn't change.

body.note: RoPE tells the model relative position ("three tokens back"), not absolute position ("token 1,207"). That suits language, where nearby words usually matter most. It's also one reason context windows can be made longer after training.

code: q, k = rope(q, m), rope(k, n)   # then q·k as usual

figure.alt: How rotary position embeddings, RoPE, mark position. First, the same vector is drawn at positions 0 to 4: at each position it is rotated by one more step, theta. Second, a query at position 5 is rotated 5 steps and a key at position 2 is rotated 2 steps, leaving an angle of 3 steps between them. Third, a query at position 9 and a key at position 6 are both rotated further, but the angle between them is again 3 steps. Because the dot product depends on that angle, the same distance between two tokens gives the same attention score, wherever they are in the text.
figure.caption: RoPE turns queries and keys by their position. Two tokens 3 apart always end up 3 steps apart in angle, so they get the same score wherever they are.
